findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async fetch_plan_limits stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is a coroutine but its body contains no `await` — `requests.get` is a synchronous, blocking call. When awaited from an async request handler it blocks the entire event loop thread for the duration of the call (up to the 5 second timeout, longer if DNS/connect stalls), so every other concurrent request on that worker stalls too. Since this runs during request handling to render remaining quota, one slow response from `billing.internal` degrades all in-flight traffic.

Use the same async client the module already depends on, e.g. `async def fetch_plan_limits(client: httpx.AsyncClient, tenant_id): response = await client.get(...)` against the billing base URL, mirroring `fetch_plan` on lines 5-7. If a sync client is genuinely required, wrap it in `anyio.to_thread.run_sync`/`loop.run_in_executor` rather than calling it directly in the coroutine. The new `import requests` on line 2 can then be dropped.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Async function makes blocking synchronous call

findings.title: New async function fetch_plan_limits has no test coverage
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is a new async function that makes a network call (via requests, synchronously) and returns parsed JSON. There is no test in this diff verifying its return value or behavior. Since the underlying issue here (sync call inside async def blocking the event loop) is a functional defect, only a test that actually awaits this coroutine under a running event loop (e.g. alongside other concurrent tasks) would reveal the blocking behavior; a naive unit test with a mocked requests.get would pass even if the blocking call stalls the loop.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is dropped straight into the path of `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}` with no quoting or type/format validation. If this value originates from a request (path segment, query string, or JSON body), a caller can supply something like `1/../../admin/tenants` or `1?x=` and redirect the call to a different endpoint on the internal billing host — a service that is presumably reachable only from the app tier and may not authorise callers strictly. `requests` does not collapse dot segments for you, so the rewritten path is sent as-is and resolved by the billing server.

Fixes, in order of preference: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. integer cast, or UUID parse) before use, and additionally pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. Also consider `allow_redirects=False` so a redirect from the internal host cannot pull the call somewhere else.

Note the pre-existing `fetch_plan` on line 6 has the same shape, so a shared validation helper would cover both.

findings.title: Bare `except:` swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
findings.body: A bare `except:` catches `BaseException`, not just `Exception`. That means `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit` raised while `_client.send` is running are quietly converted into a `None` return, so Ctrl-C or an interpreter shutdown initiated during a metrics push is ignored and execution continues. Narrow this to the failure modes you actually mean to tolerate — at minimum `except Exception:`, and preferably the transport/HTTP errors `_client.send` can raise.

findings.title: No test covers the new failure-swallowing behavior
findings.body: The change makes push_metrics catch all exceptions from _client.send and return None instead of propagating. There is no test in this diff exercising the case where _client.send raises — nothing would fail if this except block were removed, mishandled (e.g. re-raised), or if it silently swallowed an error it shouldn't (like a KeyboardInterrupt or a bug in the caller). Since the whole point of this PR is to make failures non-fatal, a test that simulates _client.send raising and asserts push_metrics returns None (and doesn't propagate) would directly validate the intended behavior.

findings.title: try_consume bypasses the lock: rate limit defeated by concurrent requests
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` (line 15), checks it against `LIMIT` (line 16), then `await asyncio.sleep(0)` (line 18) yields control to the event loop before writing back on line 19. Unlike `consume`, it never acquires `_lock`.

Adversary: any client that can drive more than one in-flight request for a tenant (the normal case for an HTTP service). What they control: request concurrency, and therefore how many coroutines sit between line 15 and line 19 at once. What they get: N concurrent calls all read the same `current`, all pass the check, and the last writer wins — so N*cost units of work are admitted while the counter advances by only `cost`. Repeating this keeps the counter arbitrarily far below the true consumption, so the limiter never trips and the noisy-client starvation the feature exists to prevent is fully reachable.

Fix: hold the same lock across the read, the check and the write, e.g. `async with _lock:` wrapping lines 15–20, and drop the `await` inside the critical section (or keep it, but only inside the lock). Reusing `consume`'s locking discipline is the minimal change.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ try_consume check-then-act races: limit bypass and lost counter updates

findings.title: No test exercises try_consume's race condition or limit logic
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters outside the lock, awaits asyncio.sleep(0) (a yield point), then writes back — a classic check-then-act race under concurrency. There is no test file in this diff, so nothing verifies either the basic limit behavior (returns False once LIMIT is exceeded) or, more importantly, that concurrent callers don't both pass the check and jointly exceed LIMIT. As written, a bug here would ship silently.

findings.title: `cost` is unvalidated; a non-positive cost would reset progress toward the limit
findings.body:
`cost` is added to the counter with no check that it is a positive number. If any caller passes a request-derived weight (a body field, a header, a batch size), a negative or zero `cost` passes the line-16 check trivially and line 19 writes back a value at or below the current one, permanently keeping the tenant under `LIMIT`. Validate at the boundary of this module: reject `cost <= 0` (and non-integers) before touching `_counters`.

I cannot see the caller, so I cannot confirm `cost` is attacker-influenced — that is the one assumption here. If it is only ever an internal constant, this is not exploitable and can be closed.

findings.title: Return shape change breaks existing tuple-unpacking caller
findings.body:
`lookup_user` previously returned a 2-tuple `(name, email)`; it now returns a dict with three keys. The existing caller `reports/weekly.py:render_row` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a dict iterates its keys, so this will raise `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call \u2014 and even if the dict had exactly two keys it would bind key strings, not values, producing silently wrong output.

Either update all callers (`render_row` \u2192 `user = lookup_user(...); user["name"], user["email"]`) in the same change, or introduce the richer shape under a new function/return type (e.g. `lookup_user_details`) and leave the tuple contract intact.

findings.title: Docstring does not match new return type
findings.body:
The docstring states `lookup_user` returns `(name, email)` as a tuple, but the function now returns a dictionary with keys `name`, `email`, and `tier`. Callers relying on the documented tuple unpacking will break—as seen in `reports/weekly.py`, which does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Update the docstring to describe the new return shape.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old (name, email) tuple contract

findings.title: Breaking return-shape change has no test to catch it
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict ({"name":..., "email":..., "tier":...}) instead of the (name, email) tuple documented in its docstring and relied on by reports/weekly.py's render_row, which does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a dict of 3 keys iterates over its keys, not (name, email), so render_row will either raise a ValueError (too many values to unpack) or silently produce wrong output depending on Python/dict semantics. No test in the diff or retrieved context exercises lookup_user's return value or render_row's behavior, so this contract break would not be caught by any existing test suite.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil after a failed INSERT
findings.body:
The error from `db.Exec` is bound to a scope-local `err` inside the `if` statement, logged, and then discarded. Lines 18-19 declare a fresh `var err error` (always nil) and return it, so `WriteSettlement` reports success even when the settlement row was never inserted. Callers of an `error`-returning function will treat nil as "written", so an end-of-day batch will silently drop settlements — and because the rows are money, the loss is not self-correcting.

Note the internal inconsistency: a validation failure on line 12-14 *is* propagated, so the function's contract is evidently to return errors; only the DB failure path is broken. Either return the insert error, or — if log-and-continue really is the intent — make that decision in the caller's loop rather than hiding it here, and document that the function cannot fail.

Suggested fix:

    if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
        log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
        return err
    }
    return nil

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Failed settlement insert is reported as success (shadowed error)

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ WriteSettlement returns nil on insert failure

findings.title: WriteSettlement has no test covering its error-return behavior
findings.body: WriteSettlement declares `var err error` at line 18 and returns it unconditionally, so it always returns nil regardless of whether the db.Exec insert on line 15 failed. No test exists for this function, so this always-nil-return behavior (and the resulting swallowed insert failures) would not be caught by any test suite. A test that calls WriteSettlement with a failing db.Exec and asserts a non-nil error is returned would catch this.

findings.title: Function name misleads about error handling
findings.body: WriteSettlement is named like WriteEntry (line 7), which returns an error from db.Exec unchanged. A caller would reasonably expect WriteSettlement to follow the same contract and return database errors. Instead, it silently logs and continues, always returning nil. The name does not communicate this exceptional behaviour — callers will assume it follows the standard pattern.

findings.title: Mutable default `attempted=[]` persists across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition, so every call that omits the argument shares the same list object. Line 10 appends failed recipients into it and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns the first call's failures as well, and the list grows without bound for the process lifetime. Callers that treat the return value as "recipients that failed in this batch" will get wrong results and may re-dispatch to recipients that already succeeded.

Use `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` and `attempted = list(attempted) if attempted is not None else []` at the top of the body \u2014 this also matches the defensive-copy idiom already used on line 2 (`dict(extra_headers or {})`).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared mutable default leaks recipients across calls and grows unbounded

findings.title: Mutable default arg bug in send_with_retries is untested
findings.body: send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=[]) uses a mutable default list, which will persist and accumulate across calls since Python evaluates default arguments once. No test exercises calling this function multiple times, so this bug (which the PR title itself references as 'cor-mutable-default-arg') would pass silently. A test that calls send_with_retries twice with failing dispatches and asserts the second call's result does not include recipients from the first call is needed to catch this.

findings.title: Mutable default argument misleads about function contract
findings.body: The function `send_with_retries` declares `attempted=[]` as a default argument. This creates a shared mutable object across all calls, which is almost never the intended behavior. A caller reading this signature would reasonably expect a fresh list each time, not a persistent accumulator. The name `attempted` and the function's apparent purpose suggest this parameter documents what the function will return, not a stateful container that persists between calls. This is a case where the signature's apparent contract contradicts what the code actually does.

findings.title: Rounding threshold silently changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5
findings.body:
The PR is described as a pure rename, but `compute_rounding` also changes the comparison operator: the old body was `return 1 if line.remainder_cents >= 0.5 else 0`, the new one is `return 1 if line.remainder_cents > 0.5 else 0`. For the exact boundary input `remainder_cents == 0.5` the function now returns 0 where it previously returned 1 — i.e. an exact half-cent now rounds down instead of up. Since this feeds monetary line-item totals, the change will produce off-by-one-cent differences on every line whose remainder lands exactly on the half, and it will not be caught by anyone reviewing this as a rename. If the behaviour change is intended, split it into its own commit with a test covering `remainder_cents == 0.5`; otherwise restore `>=`.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding boundary changed from >= to > with no test coverage

findings.title: Module docstring contradicts renamed function names
findings.body: The module docstring describes 'Line-item calculators' but all functions have been renamed from calc_* to compute_*. While semantically similar, the terminology shift should be reflected in the docstring for consistency and to avoid confusing callers about what these functions conceptually do.

findings.title: Off-by-one slice drops one record per page in page_of_sorted
findings.body:
`start` advances by a full `PAGE_SIZE` per page (line 11), but the slice end is `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1`, so each page yields only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items. The record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by any page, so a paginated export silently loses one record for every page boundary crossed. Change the slice to `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`, matching the existing `page_of` on line 6.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test covers page_of_sorted, which silently drops one record per page

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ page_of_sorted returns one fewer item than page_of

findings.title: Dropped None guard makes header_lines raise for most invoices
findings.body:
`Invoice.purchase_order` is declared `str | None` and documented as set for only about one account in twenty, so `invoice.purchase_order.upper()` on line 4 will raise `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` for the ~95% of invoices without a PO. The removed `if invoice.purchase_order is not None:` check was not redundant — the type is optional, not required. Restore the conditional append (or guard with a fallback) so the PO line is only emitted when the value is present.

Secondary contract change: the function previously returned a 1- or 2-element list; it now always returns 2 elements, so any caller that indexed or counted the result to detect the presence of a PO line will silently misbehave.

findings.title: No test exercises header_lines with purchase_order=None
findings.body: The removed guard handled invoice.purchase_order being None (per models/invoice.py docstring, true for ~19/20 accounts). The rewritten header_lines now calls .upper() unconditionally, which will raise AttributeError for the common case. There is no test in this diff, and if one existed for the None case it would now fail — but since none is shown, this regression would slip through silently.

findings.title: File handle leaks on the header-mismatch and empty-file paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` on line 10 is only closed on the success path (line 16). Two reachable paths skip it:

1. Line 13-14: when `header != expected_header` the function returns `None` with `fh` still open.
2. Line 12: `next(reader)` raises `StopIteration` on an empty file, propagating out with `fh` still open.

Rejecting bad rows is the stated purpose of this function, so the mismatch path is the *expected* path for a malformed partner catalogue, not a rare one. Under a batch import of many files this exhausts file descriptors; on CPython it is masked by refcounting, but not on PyPy and not if the handle is captured by a traceback frame.

Use the same pattern as `read_rows` on lines 4-6:

```python
def read_validated(path, expected_header):
    with open(path) as fh:
        reader = csv.reader(fh)
        header = next(reader, None)
        if header != expected_header:
            return None
        return list(reader)
```

findings.title: New read_validated function has no tests at all
findings.body: read_validated introduces branching behavior (header mismatch returns None without closing the file handle, success path returns rows) but no test file is included in this change. Nothing would catch a regression in the header-check logic, the returned row contents, or the fact that the file is left open when validation fails at line 14.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() with no idempotency key
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented as non-idempotent: "each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any transient failure *after* the gateway has already accepted the POST (timeout, connection reset on the response, 5xx emitted post-commit) will be retried and create a second (or third) real charge against the customer's card. The retry decorator cannot distinguish "request never arrived" from "response never came back".

The gateway already provides the safe path: the same docstring notes it "supports an Idempotency-Key header; pass one to make retries safe." Generate a stable key per logical charge attempt (caller-supplied, not generated inside the retry body, or it will differ per attempt) and thread it through `charge()` before retrying. Until that key exists, `charge_card` should not retry — only `fetch_charge` (a GET, documented "safe to repeat") is safe to wrap as written.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() without an Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Non-idempotent API wrapped in retry without safety contract
findings.body: The `charge_card` function wraps `gateway.charge()`, which the gateway module explicitly documents as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge" and requires an Idempotency-Key header for safe retries. The wrapper function provides no docstring and gives no indication of this requirement. A caller using `charge_card` would have no way to know that retries could create duplicate charges unless they read the underlying gateway code—the wrapper actively hides the contract.

findings.title: No test covers retry behavior around non-idempotent charge()
findings.body: charge_card wraps the non-idempotent gateway.charge() call in @retry(attempts=3). There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that exercises a transient failure followed by a retry to verify how many times the underlying charge is actually invoked. If charge() is retried after a timeout that actually succeeded server-side, nothing here would catch the resulting duplicate charge — the change ships with zero coverage on its riskiest new behavior.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body: `cutoff` is built with `datetime.now()` (no tzinfo), but `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every invite, not just edge cases. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. Note also that even if the tz mismatch were fixed, a naive `datetime.now()` returns local time, which would silently shift the cutoff by the UTC offset.

findings.title: Timezone mismatch in expires_within violates Invite.expires_at contract
findings.body: The `expires_within` function compares `invite.expires_at` (documented as timezone-aware UTC) against `datetime.now()` (timezone-naive), violating the established contract. The model documentation states that `expires_at` is always timezone-aware UTC. Line 9 uses `datetime.now()` without timezone info, which creates a naive datetime. This comparison will produce incorrect results or raise a TypeError. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` to match the contract, as already done correctly in `is_expired` on line 5.

findings.title: New expires_within() has no test covering its behavior
findings.body: expires_within mixes datetime.now() (naive) with invite.expires_at (tz-aware, per the Invite docstring), which would raise TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes at runtime. Nothing in this diff exercises this function, so this defect would ship undetected. Add a test that calls expires_within with a real Invite-like object having a tz-aware expires_at to confirm it does not raise and returns the expected boolean.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional in `web/src/types.ts` ("Absent until the customer completes onboarding."), and the adjacent `bannerFor` on line 4 already guards it with `?.` plus a default. `contactEmail` on line 8 accesses `.email` directly, so any account that has not completed onboarding will throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')`. Under `strictNullChecks` this should also fail to compile, which suggests the strict flag may be off — worth checking. Mirror the existing pattern, e.g. `return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? ""`, or change the return type to `string | undefined` and let callers handle absence.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function lacks documentation of null-dereference risk

findings.title: No test covers contactEmail with missing billingContact
findings.body: contactEmail dereferences account.billingContact.email without a null check, but Account.billingContact is optional (per web/src/types.ts). If the PR's premise that billingContact is 'always present on this page' is wrong, calling contactEmail on an account without a billing contact throws at runtime. No test exercises this function at all, so a regression or incorrect assumption would go undetected.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body:
`fetch()` documents `timeout` as MILLISECONDS and passes it straight through as `timeout_ms=timeout`. Passing `30` gives the partner API a 30ms budget, which contradicts the stated intent of a generous timeout for a slow API. The nightly job will fail (or exhaust its 3 default retries, each within the same tiny budget) on essentially every run. Use `timeout=30_000` for 30 seconds.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ fetch() timeout argument passed in seconds, not milliseconds

findings.title: Index duplicates existing invoices_tenant_created_idx from migration 0007
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_recent_idx` has exactly the same definition as `invoices_tenant_created_idx` created in migration 0007: same table, same columns, same order, same `DESC`. `IF NOT EXISTS` only matches on index *name*, so it will not suppress creation — Postgres will happily build a second, redundant index. The result is doubled write amplification and disk usage on `invoices` with no query benefit, since the planner can already use the 0007 index for the tenant + recency filter described in the PR. Drop this statement and use the existing index, or, if the intent was to replace it, explicitly drop `invoices_tenant_created_idx`.

findings.title: priority=9 delays reset email; scale is inverted (0 drains first)
findings.body:
`enqueue`'s docstring states the priority argument is an ordering index where **0 is drained first and 9 is drained last**, explicitly warning that the name suggests the opposite. Passing `priority=9` therefore puts password-reset mail behind every other queued job, including the nightly digest batch this PR is trying to jump ahead of. It is also strictly worse than the previous behaviour, which used the default of 5.

Use `priority=0` (or a small value) to drain reset mail ahead of digests.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ priority=9 delays reset mail instead of prioritising it

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ priority=9 deprioritizes reset email, contradicting stated goal

findings.title: Priority 9 queues resets last, contradicting PR intent
findings.body: The diff sets password reset email priority to 9, but the priority system documentation (queue/priority.py) explicitly states that priority 0 is drained first and 9 is drained last. This means password resets will now queue *behind* the nightly digest batch, not ahead of it as the PR description claims. Either the priority value is wrong (should be 0 for highest priority) or the PR intent description is wrong.

findings.title: Indexed terms not normalized; will be unfindable by search
findings.body: The call to `upsert(article.id, article.title.split())` passes the title terms directly without lowercasing or deduplicating them. The `upsert` function's docstring explicitly states: "a term differing only by case creates a second posting list, and queries — which do lower-case — will never match it. The document then indexes successfully and is silently unfindable by that term." This means articles will be indexed but unfindable by any query unless the search term exactly matches the case of the title.

findings.title: upsert called with un-normalised title terms
findings.body:
`upsert` documents that `terms` must already be lower-cased and de-duplicated, and explicitly states that it does not normalise them — a term differing only by case creates a second posting list that lower-casing queries will never match. `article.title.split()` yields the raw words of the title, so a title like "The Quick Fox" indexes `The`, `Quick`, `Fox` and none of them are reachable from search. The document indexes without error, so the failure is silent.

Normalise at the call site, e.g. `upsert(article.id, {w.lower() for w in article.title.split()})` (or push the normalisation into `upsert` if that is the better home for it).

findings.title: No test covers that indexed terms must be normalised before upsert
findings.body: upsert()'s docstring explicitly warns that terms must be lower-cased and de-duplicated before calling it, and that failing to do so makes the document silently unfindable by that term. The new call at publish/articles.py:7 passes article.title.split() directly, which is neither lower-cased nor de-duplicated. There is no test in this change that publishes an article with a mixed-case title and then queries the search index to confirm the term is findable — such a test would fail today given the current call, since a query for the lower-cased term would not match the indexed mixed-case term.

findings.title: Referer logged unscrubbed, leaking auth token into logs
findings.body:
Line 5 now assigns `request.headers[header]` directly for every header, dropping the `Referer`-specific `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` call that the previous code applied. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `f"{base}?token={token}"`, and the browser sends that full URL back in the `Referer` header on every subresource request. On any 5xx the raw Referer — including `?token=<auth token>` — is serialised by `json.dumps` into the log at line 6, so anyone with log read access (or log shipping/aggregation downstream) obtains a working credential.

Restore the conditional scrub before storing the value:

```python
value = request.headers[header]
if header == "Referer":
    value = _scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)
headers[header] = value
```

Note also that after this change `extra_param_keys` appears to have no remaining use in this function, which is a further signal that the sanitisation path was dropped rather than intentionally relocated.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token leaks into logs: Referer scrubbing removed

findings.title: No test guards Referer scrubbing in header logging
findings.body: The change deletes the call to _scrub_uri for the Referer header, which per jupyter_server/auth/identity.py exists specifically because notebook URLs embed the auth token and browsers echo it back in Referer. If this removal is wrong (i.e. it reintroduces token leakage into logs), no test in this diff or apparently in the surrounding suite would fail — there is no assertion anywhere checking that a Referer containing `?token=...` is redacted before being logged. Add a test that logs a request with a token-bearing Referer and asserts the emitted JSON does not contain the raw token.

findings.title: xlinkhref no longer scheme-checked, reopening script-URI injection
findings.body:
Previously `attribute === 'xlinkhref'` routed the value into `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)`, which rejects the `unsafeLinkPrefix` schemes (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After this change `xlinkhref` misses that branch and falls through to whatever the function's default outcome is at the end — which, for an attribute that is still emitted, means an unvalidated URL. `<a xlink:href="javascript:...">` inside SVG is a live navigation vector in browsers, so author/user-submitted markdown can now execute script.

The PR description says the intent is to drop rarely used SVG attributes, but the diff only deletes the *validation* branch; it does not remove `xlink:href` from any attribute allowlist. If the attribute really is being dropped, remove it where it is permitted and leave the scheme check intact (a redundant check is harmless); if it is still permitted, restore the `attribute === 'xlinkhref'` clause.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ xlink:href no longer scheme-checked, re-enabling SVG javascript: XSS

findings.title: No test guards removal of 'xlinkhref' from sanitised attributes
findings.body: The diff removes 'xlinkhref' from the list of attributes routed through isAnchorLinkAllowed, meaning xlink:href values (e.g. on SVG <a> or <use> elements) are no longer validated against unsafeLinkPrefix. If this regresses (e.g. is reintroduced insecurely, or someone assumes xlinkhref is still checked elsewhere), nothing in the test suite would catch it. No test file is part of this change to confirm xlinkhref is now unchecked-by-design versus accidentally broken.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID lets project query param traverse out of storage root
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string and, after this change, reaches the DAO layer with no identifier check. The file DAO's `buildPath` is documented as doing no validation of its own — "callers are required to have validated the names before this point" — and `filepath.Join` normalises rather than confines: `filepath.Join(d.Folder, "../../etc", kind)` resolves outside `d.Folder`. The PR rationale that "the path join already scopes under the folder root" does not hold for Go's `filepath.Join`.

The remaining check on line 4 only compares the query value against the path value; when `parameters.Project` is empty it performs no validation at all, so the traversal payload passes through unchanged. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` call (or move an equivalent check into `buildPath`) before the value is used to build a filesystem path.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removed project-name validation enables path traversal in file DAO

findings.title: No test covers removal of project-name validation in list()
findings.body: The diff removes the call to common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter), which previously rejected malformed/malicious project identifiers (e.g. containing path separators like '../') before they reached buildPath. No test in this change exercises list() with such a value to confirm the path-join scoping in buildPath actually prevents traversal, nor does any test assert the old bad-request behavior is intentionally gone. If the assumption that filepath.Join scoping is sufficient turns out to be wrong, no test would fail — the change would silently ship an unvalidated path segment into disk I/O.

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from unvalidated client Content-Length
findings.body:
`contentLength` on this path is the declared length of the incoming part request, i.e. an attacker-controlled header value, and it is now handed straight to `Reserve` before a single byte of `body` has been read. Previously the RW grew page-by-page as `io.Copy` actually consumed data, so the memory committed was bounded by the bytes really delivered; now a request that declares a huge Content-Length and then sends nothing (or trickles bytes) commits that allocation up front. A handful of concurrent such requests exhausts the process. Clamp the reservation to a sane ceiling (e.g. `min(contentLength, maxPartSize)` and skip reserving entirely for values above it) so the declared size is only ever a hint for an allocation you were willing to make anyway, and keep relying on the copy for the real growth.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Buffer pre-reserved from client-declared Content-Length without a cap

findings.title: No test exercises the new Reserve(contentLength) behaviour
findings.body: The change adds pre-allocation of the multipart buffer based on contentLength via Reserve(contentLength). This is exactly the kind of change (declared-length-driven allocation) that motivated this eval, yet no test verifies that: (1) a correct Content-Length still produces a correct upload/ETag, or (2) an attacker-controlled or mismatched Content-Length (e.g., very large declared length with small actual body, or negative/zero) does not cause excessive allocation or a panic. If Reserve mishandles an untrusted or mismatched contentLength, nothing in this diff or the visible surrounding code would catch it.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme silently changes from https to http
findings.body:
The original expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only selected `http` when a caller explicitly set `is_secure = False`; a missing key (`.get` returns `None`) fell through to `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats the missing key as falsy, so every request that does not explicitly set `request.meta["is_secure"] = True` is now sent over plaintext HTTP to `{bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com`, carrying the AWS request signature and any object data unencrypted. This is not an equivalent simplification.

If the goal is a single ternary, preserve the secure default, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` (unchanged), or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`. Note the second form also changes behaviour for falsy-but-not-False values such as `0` or `""`, which previously yielded `https`.

findings.title: S3 requests now default to plaintext HTTP when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` was fail-secure: only an explicit `is_secure=False` opted into plaintext; a missing key (the common case, since `request.meta` need not carry the flag) yielded `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats a missing key — and any falsy value such as `None` or `""` — as a request for `http`, so the URL built on line 6 becomes `http://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/...`.

S3 downloads carry AWS authorization material (signed `Authorization`/`x-amz-*` headers or presigned query parameters) plus the object body. Sending them over cleartext exposes them to any on-path observer.

Fix: restore the fail-secure default, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or normalise with `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)` so only an explicit opt-out downgrades the transport.

findings.title: Default scheme behavior change is untested
findings.body: The old logic defaulted to https unless is_secure was explicitly False; the new logic defaults to http unless is_secure is truthy. This changes behavior for the common case where is_secure is not set (e.g. missing from request.meta), silently downgrading requests from https to http by default. No test exercises download_request with is_secure absent/None vs explicitly True/False, so this regression (which is also a security concern) would not be caught by any test suite.

findings.title: DELETE now authorizes as "push", granting delete to push-only accounts
findings.body:
The previous switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the `delete` action; the new two-branch form sends every non-GET/HEAD method — including DELETE — down the `action = "push"` path. The resulting `ResourceAction{Name: name, Action: action}` is what the access-control layer evaluates, so a DELETE on `/v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>` is now checked against the caller's *push* grant. Per `pkg/api/config/config.go`, the actions are separate precisely so "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones" — that separation is now unenforceable, and the `delete` action becomes dead configuration that silently grants nothing while push silently grants destruction.

Adversary: any authenticated principal (or anonymous principal, if the policy grants anonymous push) holding only `push` on a repository. What they control: the HTTP method and the `name`/reference path variables. What they get: deletion of manifests/tags they were explicitly not authorized to remove — irreversible data loss and a supply-chain foothold (delete a tag, re-push a different image under it).

Restore the explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch before the catch-all.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ DELETE now authorises as "push", dropping the delete permission check

findings.title: No test covers that DELETE now maps to 'push' instead of 'delete'
findings.body: The change removes the distinct ActionDelete mapping for http.MethodDelete, folding it into 'push'. This is a meaningful authorization behavior change (per the repo's own documented rationale that push and delete should be distinct), yet no test in this diff exercises the DELETE case to confirm/catch this. If this mapping is wrong, nothing in the current change would fail.

findings.title: Default for unrecognised methods flipped from "pull" to "push"
findings.body: The old `default:` arm mapped any method outside the enumerated set (e.g. OPTIONS, TRACE, or a custom verb) to `"pull"`. The new inverted condition sends all of them to `"push"`, so read-only or preflight-style requests from pull-only accounts will now be rejected. If the permissive default was intentional, enumerate the write methods explicitly rather than negating the read methods.

findings.title: Size guard clears the whole cache, including the entry just stored
findings.body:
When `_CACHE` grows past 1000, the entire shared dict is discarded rather than evicting a single entry. Two consequences: (a) every other tenant's cached value is destroyed, so unrelated `get_tenant` callers start returning `None` in a burst; (b) because `clear()` runs *after* the insertion on line 10, the tenant that was just fetched is also dropped, so an immediate `get_tenant(tenant_id)` after `get_tenant_fresh(tenant_id)` returns `None` even though the fresh value was supposedly warmed into the cache. If a bounded cache is the intent, evict a single/oldest entry (e.g. an LRU or `popitem`) instead of flushing, and re-insert or check the size before storing.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Size bound flushes the whole shared cache instead of evicting

findings.title: Function name `get_tenant_fresh` contradicts its mutating behavior
findings.body: The function name `get_tenant_fresh` reads as a getter — a read-only operation that retrieves a value. However, the function mutates the shared `_CACHE` state by writing to it (line 10) and potentially clearing it (line 12). A caller expecting read-only semantics could be surprised by these side effects. Consider a name like `fetch_and_cache_tenant` or `refresh_tenant_cache` that signals the function performs writes.

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh has no test coverage for cache write or eviction logic
findings.body: The new function fetches a tenant, writes it into _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this diff includes a test, so a bug in the eviction threshold (off-by-one, wrong comparison, clearing instead of evicting oldest) or in the write-through behaviour (e.g. forgetting to update _CACHE) would not be caught by anything in the repository as shown.

findings.title: Documentation references renamed flag --workers
findings.body: Line 7 documents `--workers` but the CLI flag has been renamed to `--concurrency` in cli.py line 6. A user reading the README will try to use `--workers`, which no longer exists. Update the documentation to reflect the new flag name.

findings.title: Flag rename breaks existing invocations and `args.workers` readers
findings.body:
Renaming `--workers` to `--concurrency` changes two contracts at once:

1. Any existing script, Makefile, CI job or container entrypoint passing `--workers N` will now fail with `unrecognized arguments`, since argparse offers no alias.
2. The argparse destination changes too — the namespace attribute is now `args.concurrency`, not `args.workers`. Every consumer of `parser()`'s result that reads `args.workers` will raise `AttributeError` at runtime, and this diff touches only the flag declaration, not any consumer.

If the rename is intended, either keep the old spelling as an accepted alias (`p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", type=int, default=4)`) for a deprecation period, or update every call site that reads `args.workers` in the same change. The README hunk in this PR still documents `--workers` (README.md line 7), which suggests the rename was not carried through everywhere.

findings.title: Docstring does not match changed return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation on line 4 now returns a dictionary mapping day to count. A caller writing `total = monthly_usage(account_id)` and then using `total + 1` would break immediately. Update the docstring to reflect the new return contract: a dict with day as key and count as value.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict; callers still expect an integer
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns a `{day: count}` mapping. Any existing caller doing arithmetic, comparison, or formatting on the result (e.g. `if monthly_usage(a) > limit`) will now silently compare against a dict or raise a `TypeError`. The docstring on line 2 still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", which confirms no caller-side contract was renegotiated in this change. Either keep a total-returning function and add a new per-day function, or update every call site and the docstring together.

findings.title: No test covers the new per-day breakdown return shape
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict mapping day to count instead of a single integer total, but no test file is included in this diff. Any caller relying on the old return contract, or a bug in the GROUP BY/dict-comprehension logic (e.g. wrong key names, missing days, incorrect aggregation), would not be caught by any existing test. Add a test that calls monthly_usage against a fixture with multiple days of data and asserts the returned dict has the correct per-day keys and counts.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` is a public-looking API function whose second parameter changed name from `page_size` to `limit`. Any existing caller written as `list_invoices(tid, page_size=100)` now raises `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'` at runtime — positional callers are unaffected, which is exactly what makes this easy to miss in testing. No callers were retrieved for this review, so the blast radius is unverified. Either grep the repository for `page_size=` and update every call site in this PR, or accept the old name for a deprecation window (e.g. `def list_invoices(tenant_id, limit=50, cursor=None, page_size=None)` mapping the legacy value onto `limit` with a warning).

findings.title: Docstring still documents the removed page_size parameter
findings.body:
The Args block still lists `page_size:` while the signature now takes `limit`. Anyone reading the docstring (or generated API docs) will write `page_size=...` and hit the `TypeError` described above. Update the docstring entry to `limit: how many invoices to return.`

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Docstring parameter name does not match signature

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is an absolute import of a package module
findings.body: Every other import in this module is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will only resolve if a top-level module named `adapters` happens to be on `sys.path`; under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `absolute_import`) importing `requests.sessions` raises `ImportError` outright. Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: `_send_request` deleted but `old_request` still calls it
findings.body: The `_send_request` helper was removed in this diff, yet the retained `old_request` body still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call path that reaches `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep the helper until `old_request` is deleted, or inline `r.send(prefetch=...)`/`return r.response` at the call site.

findings.title: New `request()` silently drops timeout/verify/cert/prefetch/config and session defaults
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public signature but only forwards `method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies, hooks` onto the `Request`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `config` and `return_response` are accepted and then discarded — callers (e.g. `requests.api.request`/`get`/`post`, which pass `timeout` and `verify`) will silently get unverified TLS defaults, no timeout, and a response object regardless of `return_response=False`. Equally, nothing merges the session-level `self.headers`, `self.auth`, `self.cookies`, `self.params` or `self.config` into the request any more, so `Session(headers=...)` stops having any effect. Silently ignoring a parameter is worse than raising; wire them through or `raise NotImplementedError` while the refactor is in flight.

findings.title: A new HTTPAdapter (and pool) is built per send(); close() no longer releases anything
findings.body: `send()` instantiates a fresh `HTTPAdapter()` on every call. Assuming the adapter owns a `PoolManager` (that is the point of moving pooling off `Session`), this creates a new connection pool per request, so keep-alive/connection reuse is gone and sockets accumulate until GC. At the same time `close()` was reduced to `pass`, so `with Session() as s:` and explicit `s.close()` no longer release any pooled connections. Hold a single adapter on the session (e.g. built in `__init__` from `pool_connections`/`pool_maxsize`) and have `close()` delegate to it.

findings.title: verify/cert silently dropped on new request path (TLS settings ignored)
close() no longer disposes resources, and nothing verifies it
findings.body: close() previously cleared the PoolManager to release pooled connections; it is now a no-op (`pass`) since Session no longer owns a poolmanager. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that exercises close() and asserts connections/resources are actually released, so this silent behaviour loss — sessions no longer freeing pooled connections — would not be caught by any test.

findings.title: send() now delegates to a new HTTPAdapter with no test verifying request actually gets sent/response returned correctly
findings.body: send() changed from `return request.send()` to constructing an `HTTPAdapter()` per call and delegating to it. This is the core of the 'move sending onto an HTTPAdapter' refactor, yet no test in the diff exercises Session.send() or Session.request() end-to-end to confirm a PreparedRequest is still sent and a Response returned as before. A regression in the adapter wiring (e.g., wrong request object passed, response not returned) would pass silently.

findings.title: Stale docstring removed from close() without updating contract
findings.body: The `close()` method previously had a docstring explaining it "closes the PoolManager, which closes pooled connections." That docstring has been removed, but the method body now contains only `pass`, meaning the documented behavior no longer occurs. Callers who expect `close()` to clean up resources based on the old documentation will be surprised. Either restore the docstring and implement the promised cleanup, or add a new docstring explaining that `close()` is now a no-op.

findings.title: Top-level `from adapters import ...` resolves outside the package
findings.body: Every other import in this module is package-relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is absolute, so under Python 3 (and Python 2 with `absolute_import`) it resolves against `sys.path` rather than the `requests` package. Any `adapters.py` earlier on `sys.path` — notably the process working directory, which is on `sys.path` for scripts and `python -m` — is imported instead, and that module then handles every outbound request, including TLS setup and credentials. Adversary: anyone who can place a file in a directory the application is launched from (shared build agents, world-writable app dirs, a user-writable CWD); they control the module body and get code execution inside the HTTP client. Change to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: send() docstring does not document adapter instantiation side effect
findings.body: The `send()` method creates a new HTTPAdapter on every call (line 365). This could be a significant behavioral contract worth documenting—callers should understand that each send spawns a new adapter rather than reusing a session-level adapter. The docstring "Send a given PreparedRequest." is too vague to convey this.

findings.title: cookies returns None on parse failure, breaking all callers
findings.body:
On a malformed `Cookie` header the `except` branch assigns `self._cookies = None` and the property returns `None`. Because `_cookies` is now set, every later access returns `None` too. The callers updated in this same PR assume a dict-like object: `if name in self.request.cookies` (web.py:321) raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, and `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (web.py:367) raises `AttributeError`. The previous implementation left `self._cookies` as a `SimpleCookie` and called `clear_all_cookies()`, so the property always returned a mapping. Since `HTTPRequest` has no response-side access, the fix is to reset to an empty container instead: `self._cookies = Cookie.SimpleCookie()` (or `self._cookies.clear()`) in the `except` block.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, causing 500s

findings.title: Moved cookies property, including a behavior change on parse failure, has no test
findings.body: The new HTTPRequest.cookies property changes what happens when Cookie.load() raises: previously RequestHandler.cookies called self.clear_all_cookies() on failure (leaving self.cookies as an empty/valid SimpleCookie), now the property sets self._cookies = None on failure. Downstream callers get_cookie() and clear_all_cookies() (tornado/web.py lines 321 and 367) assume a dict-like object and would raise a TypeError/AttributeError if cookies is None. Nothing in this diff exercises a malformed Cookie header, so this regression would not be caught by any existing or added test.

findings.title: Incomplete docstring for HTTPRequest.cookies property
findings.body: The docstring states the property returns 'A dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects', but the implementation can return `None` when cookie parsing fails (line 523). Callers who treat this as a dictionary without checking for None will break. The docstring should document this exceptional case.

findings.title: RequestHandler.cookies removed without a delegating alias
findings.body: `RequestHandler.cookies` was a documented public property; application subclasses and templates that read `self.cookies` / `handler.cookies` will now raise `AttributeError` after this move. Consider keeping a thin property on `RequestHandler` that returns `self.request.cookies` so existing callers keep working while request-level code gets direct access.

findings.title: Boundary parameter name not stripped; breaks normal multipart uploads
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` leaves the optional whitespace that clients put after the separator, so for the standard header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz` the second fragment is `" boundary=----..."` and `k` is `" boundary"`. The comparison `k == "boundary"` on line 363 is therefore false, the loop finishes without `break`, and the `for`/`else` on line 366 logs "Invalid multipart/form-data" instead of parsing the body. Every browser-generated file upload silently loses its form fields — a regression from the previous `'boundary=' in content_type` test, which tolerated the space.

Normalise the fragment before comparing, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` and compare `k.lower() == "boundary"` (RFC 2045 parameter names are case-insensitive, so `Boundary=` would also be missed today). Stripping surrounding double quotes from `v` would additionally handle the RFC-permitted `boundary="..."` quoted form, though that shortcoming predates this change.

findings.title: Boundary parameter parsed without trimming or unquoting Content-Type params
findings.body:
Entry point: the client-supplied `Content-Type` request header (fully attacker controlled). Sink: the `boundary` value chosen here and handed to `self._parse_mime_body`, which decides how the request body is split into fields/files.

Each `;`-separated parameter is matched with `field.partition("=")` and compared with `k == "boundary"` without normalisation. Per RFC 2045/2046 a parameter may be preceded by linear whitespace and its value may be a quoted string, so:

- `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc` yields `k == " boundary"` and is skipped, falling through to the `else` warning — the body is silently not parsed.
- `multipart/form-data;boundary="abc"` yields `v == '"abc"'`, so the quotes become part of the delimiter and no parts match.

Besides dropping legitimate uploads, this makes Tornado's parameter parsing differ from that of any proxy, WAF or upload scanner in front of it. An attacker who can reach the server can send e.g. `multipart/form-data; boundary=A;boundary=B`: a normalising intermediary inspects the body framed by `A`, while this loop skips `" boundary=A"` and parses with `B`, so the fields the application actually sees are not the ones that were inspected — a content-inspection bypass with no special client required.

Fix: normalise before comparing, i.e. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, and strip surrounding double quotes from `v`; consider rejecting requests that carry more than one `boundary` parameter rather than taking the first match.

findings.title: No test exercises multipart boundary parsing with non-last 'boundary=' field
findings.body: The change fixes a bug where 'boundary=' was assumed to be the last parameter in the Content-Type header. No test in this diff exercises a Content-Type header like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=X; charset=utf-8' (boundary not last) to verify the fix actually works and to catch a future regression back to the old split-based logic.

findings.title: get_host URL parsing logic has no test coverage in this change
findings.body: get_host implements custom URL parsing (scheme/host/port extraction, port validation, error raising on non-digit port) but no test exercises it as part of this diff. A regression in the split logic (e.g. order of scheme/path/auth/port stripping) or the error path (LocationParseError with unformatted %s) would not be caught.

findings.title: get_host ignores '?' and '#' delimiters, diverging from urlparse on host
findings.body:
`get_host` strips the scheme, then everything after the first `/`, then everything before the last-seen `@`. It never treats `?` or `#` as terminating the authority, so `http://good.example.com#@attacker.tld/` is parsed as host `attacker.tld`, while `urllib.parse.urlsplit` on the same string reports netloc `good.example.com` (the `#@attacker.tld/` is the fragment). The same divergence occurs with `?` (`http://good.example.com?@attacker.tld/`).

Adversary: a user who can submit a URL to a service that fetches it (webhook registration, avatar/link fetcher, SSRF-guarded proxy). What they control: the whole URL string. What they get: the service's allowlist check — typically written against `urlparse`/`urlsplit` — passes on `good.example.com`, but the connection this helper drives goes to `attacker.tld` or to an internal address, i.e. an SSRF/allowlist bypass.

Fix: terminate the authority on the first of `/`, `?`, or `#` before the `@` and `:` handling, e.g. split on a character class rather than `/` alone, or delegate to `urlsplit` and read `.hostname`/`.port`.

Note this is a property of the helper as lifted, not something the refactor introduced; raising it because this is the moment the function becomes the single shared entry point every caller imports.

findings.title: LocationParseError message has an unsubstituted %s placeholder
findings.body: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` never interpolates the URL, so every parse failure surfaces the literal string `Failed to parse: %s` with no indication of which input failed — the one piece of information the caller needs to debug. Change to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or pass the original url, since `url` has already been stripped of scheme/path/auth by this point).

findings.title: accept_encoding unicode string silently replaced with 'gzip,deflate' on py2
findings.body: The type dispatch tests `isinstance(accept_encoding, str)`. On Python 2 a `unicode` value (e.g. from a module with `from __future__ import unicode_literals`, or any decoded config value) is neither `str` nor `list`, so it falls into the `else` branch and the caller-supplied encoding is silently discarded and replaced with `'gzip,deflate'` — a wrong header rather than an error. Since `six` is already imported in this module, `isinstance(accept_encoding, six.string_types)` fixes it.

findings.title: No test covers sort="status"
findings.body: SORTABLE defines three columns (created_at, amount, status) but the tests only exercise created_at (default) and amount. If the mapping for "status" were wrong (e.g. mapped to the wrong column or broke query building), nothing in the test suite would catch it.

findings.title: describe() has no test exercising either branch
findings.body: The change removes type-cast workarounds and relies on TypeScript's discriminated-union narrowing to guarantee `event.x` and `event.code` are valid at runtime. There is no test file in this diff or referenced that calls `describe()` with a click event and a key event to confirm the returned strings are correct. If a future edit renamed a field (e.g., `x` to `posX`) or broke the discriminant check, this would only be caught by the TypeScript compiler, not by a runtime test — and if `event.kind` were ever a value neither branch expects, the current code would silently return the key branch's template. Consider adding a small unit test asserting `describe()` output for both event kinds.

findings.title: HTTPMove.location changes from str to URL, breaking documented contract
findings.body:
`self.location` was previously the exact string passed to the constructor; it is now a `yarl.URL` instance. The documented contract (docs/web_reference.rst) states the attribute is "the string it was constructed with" and that application code compares it against configured strings and calls `str.startswith` on it. After this change:

- `exc.location.startswith("/admin")` raises `AttributeError` (URL has no `startswith`).
- `exc.location == "/login"` silently evaluates to `False` rather than `True`, because `URL.__eq__` does not compare equal to a plain `str` — a silent behaviour change that no test or exception will surface.
- Even `str(exc.location)` is not guaranteed to round-trip the input, since `URL()` normalises (percent-encoding, default-port stripping, path normalisation).

If the goal is just to avoid parsing twice, keep the attribute as the original value and use a local: `url = URL(location); self.headers['Location'] = str(url); self.location = location`. If exposing a `URL` is intended, it is a breaking public API change that needs a separate attribute (e.g. `location_url`) or a deprecation cycle plus a docs update.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ `.location` type change can silently defeat redirect-target allowlist checks

findings.title: HTTPMove.location now returns URL object, not string
findings.body:
The `location` attribute is now assigned a `URL(location)` object (line 8) instead of the raw string `location`. However, the documented contract in `docs/web_reference.rst` states it is 'the string it was constructed with' and that 'Application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`'. This documentation is now incorrect — callers expecting a string will receive a URL object instead, and string methods like `str.startswith` will not work as documented.

Either revert the assignment to store the string, or update the documentation in `docs/web_reference.rst` to reflect that `location` is now a `URL` object.

findings.title: No test guards self.location's documented string type
findings.body: self.location now stores a URL object instead of the original string, contradicting the documented contract ('as the string it was constructed with', per docs/web_reference.rst) that application code relies on for str.startswith comparisons. There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the existing suite) that asserts isinstance(exc.location, str) or checks value equality against the original string, so this behavior change would pass silently.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after while→if change
findings.body:
`_wait()` is explicitly documented as resolving "at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." Replacing the `while` loop with a single `if` removes exactly that re-check: after the spurious wake, control falls through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` with an empty buffer and `self._eof` still false, so `readany()` returns `b""`.

An empty return from `readany()` is the documented EOF sentinel, so consumers looping `while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break` will silently truncate the stream mid-body. Restore the `while` so the condition is re-evaluated on every wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ readany() can return b"" before EOF, letting a peer truncate a body

findings.title: No test covers the while→if change for spurious wakeups
findings.body: The docstring for _wait explicitly warns that the waiter can be resolved at the end of a chunk with no new data, so callers must re-check their condition after waking. This change replaces the re-checking while loop with a single if, meaning readany() will return early with an empty result if the wait resolves without new data. No test in this diff exercises a spurious/no-data wakeup scenario, so a regression (returning empty buffer prematurely) would not be caught by existing tests.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` breaks package import
findings.body: `adapters` is a sibling module inside the `requests` package, not a top-level module. With Python 3 (and Python 2 with `from __future__ import absolute_import`), `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is resolved against `sys.path`, not against the containing package, so it raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` unless the caller happens to have `requests/` itself on `sys.path`. Since `sessions` is imported during `import requests`, this makes the whole library unimportable for every consumer. It is also inconsistent with the adjacent relative import on line 6 (`from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` (or use the fully qualified `from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter`).

findings.title: Implicit import lets any sys.path entry shadow HTTPAdapter
findings.body:
`from adapters import HTTPAdapter` no longer binds to `requests.adapters`; under Python 2 (where implicit relative imports still resolve) it is looked up through `sys.path` — including `sys.path[0]`, the directory of the running script, and any other writable entry such as a shared deployment directory or a `PYTHONPATH` element. An attacker who can drop an `adapters.py` into any of those directories controls the class that every `Session` uses to mount transport adapters: they get arbitrary code execution at import time and full control over TLS verification, proxying and request/response handling for all traffic in the process. Restore the explicit relative form (`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`) so resolution is pinned to the package and cannot be influenced by `sys.path`.

Note also that on Python 3 this form does not resolve to the package at all, so the shadowing case is not hypothetical there — the only way it imports successfully is via an unrelated top-level `adapters` module.

findings.title: Removing None guard makes get_cookie raise on unparsable Cookie header
findings.body:
`self.request.cookies` is not always a mapping. The `HTTPRequest.cookies` property returns `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but cannot be parsed, and its docstring states that "every consumer has to allow for that". With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, so a malformed client-supplied cookie header turns every `get_cookie` call into a 500 instead of returning `default`.

Either restore the `is not None` check, or make `HTTPRequest.cookies` return an empty dict on parse failure (and update its docstring and any callers that test for `None`) before simplifying here.

findings.title: Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header raise TypeError
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented (and implemented) to return `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but cannot be parsed. With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Adversary: any unauthenticated remote client. What they control: the raw `Cookie` request header. What they get: an unhandled exception inside `get_cookie`, which surfaces as a 500 on every handler that reads a cookie — including the XSRF and secure-cookie paths that call `get_cookie` during authentication/validation. A single trivially-crafted header turns those endpoints into errors, and any handler code that expected `get_cookie` to return `default` on bad input now gets an exception instead of a safe fallback.

Restore the guard (`if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`), or fix it at the source by having the `cookies` property return an empty mapping instead of `None` and updating the docstring accordingly.

findings.title: Removed None-guard for cookies has no test covering unparseable Cookie header
findings.body: get_cookie now does `if name in self.request.cookies` without checking for None first. Per tornado/httpserver.py's cookies property docstring, self._cookies (and thus request.cookies) is set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed. This change would raise a TypeError in that case instead of returning default, but no test exercises get_cookie with a request that has an unparseable Cookie header, so this regression would go undetected.

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks boundary detection after "; " separator
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` leaves the conventional whitespace that follows the semicolon on each parameter, so for the standard header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundary` the loop sees the field `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundary"`. `field.partition("=")` then yields `k == " boundary"`, and the check on line 5 (`k == "boundary"`) is false, so `_parse_mime_body` is never called and the `break` never fires. Every multipart/form-data upload sent with the usual `"; "` separator would silently parse to an empty body — no exception, just lost fields and files. The strip was not redundant: it normalised both the parameter name and (via the partition on the stripped string) trailing whitespace/CRLF on the value. Restore it, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, or strip `k` and `v` individually before comparing.

findings.title: Dropping strip() makes multipart parsing depend on attacker whitespace
findings.body:
`content_type` comes straight from the client's `Content-Type` request header. After `content_type.split(";")`, every parameter except the first retains the leading space that conventionally follows the semicolon, so for the ordinary header `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc` the loop computes `k == " boundary"`, the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 fails, and `_parse_mime_body` is never called — the body is silently discarded. Only the space-less spelling `multipart/form-data;boundary=abc` still parses.

The adversary is any client that can set its own `Content-Type`; what they control is a single space character; what they get is control over whether Tornado parses the multipart body at all. That is a parsing differential against anything in front of or beside the handler that does parse the body per RFC 7231 (a WAF, reverse proxy, upload scanner, or middleware that inspects fields): the attacker can present a body the filter sees and validates while Tornado sees no arguments, or vice versa, and handler logic that branches on "argument absent" (defaults, optional-field paths) then runs on input the filter believed it had cleared.

A secondary effect on the same lines: previously `field.strip()` also removed trailing whitespace, so `v` was clean; now `boundary=abc ` yields `v == "abc "`, which is passed unmodified to `_parse_mime_body` on line 6 as the boundary.

Restore the strip, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, or strip `k` and `v` individually.

findings.title: No test covers boundary parsing with leading whitespace after removing strip()
findings.body: The change drops `.strip()` before `partition("=")`, so `k` will now retain leading whitespace when a header field looks like `multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz` (common formatting with a space after the semicolon). Previously `k.strip()` normalized this to `"boundary"`; now `k` would be `" boundary"`, which fails the `k == "boundary"` check and silently skips multipart parsing. No test in this PR (or apparently in the existing suite) exercises a Content-Type header with a space after the semicolon, so this behavior change would not be caught by any test run.

findings.title: Format string has placeholder but no argument provided
findings.body:
The error message on line 7 contains a `%s` format placeholder but no argument is provided to fill it. This will result in a TypeError at runtime when this exception is raised. The previous code passed `url` as the argument; if the intention is to remove the URL from the message, the placeholder should also be removed. If the intention is to keep the URL, the argument must be restored.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error message left with literal '%s' placeholder, losing the URL

findings.title: No test exercises the LocationParseError formatting path
findings.body: The edited line changes `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")`, dropping the substitution argument. This will raise `TypeError: not enough arguments for format string` the next time a non-digit port triggers this branch, instead of raising the intended LocationParseError. No test in this diff (and none retrieved from the repo) calls the URL-parsing function with a malformed port to hit this branch, so this regression would not be caught by the existing suite.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation into shell=True misbehaves and executes input
findings.body:
`cmd` is built by string interpolation and run with `shell=True`, so `name` and `directory` are parsed by the shell rather than passed as single argv entries. Two concrete consequences for reachable inputs:

1. Correctness: `directory="my reports"` becomes two tar operands, so tar archives `my` and `reports` (or fails with "Cannot stat"), never the intended directory. Likewise `name="Q1 2024"` writes `/exports/Q1` and treats `2024.tar.gz` as an input path.
2. Any shell metacharacter in either argument is honoured, so `name` of `x; rm -rf /exports` runs a second command with the process's privileges.

Both go away with the same fix used by `list_exports` on line 5 — pass an argument list and drop the shell:

```python
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)
```

and validate `name` against a whitelist (e.g. no `/` or `..`) so it cannot escape `/exports`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Command injection via shell=True in create_archive

findings.title: No test coverage for create_archive command construction
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. There is no test exercising this function, so a change to the command format, quoting, or the shell=True behavior (e.g. failing to sanitize name/directory, or breaking the tar invocation) would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: create_archive returns CompletedProcess, unlike sibling which returns stdout
findings.body: `list_exports` returns `.stdout` (bytes), while `create_archive` returns the whole `CompletedProcess` object. If callers of this module treat the return value uniformly (e.g. decoding it, or returning it in a response body), `create_archive` will hand back a repr of a `CompletedProcess` instead of output. Consider returning the archive path (`f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz"`) or `None`, so the contract is explicit rather than an incidental subprocess object.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin with credentials enabled on dashboard routes
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, discarding the `ALLOWED` allowlist used by the existing middleware two lines above. Any route that mounts `dashboardCors` is reachable cross-origin from every site on the internet.

Adversary: any web page a logged-in user visits. What they control: a `fetch()`/XHR from their own origin to this API, including the `Origin` header. What they get: the response body of API endpoints served under this middleware — i.e. whatever the dashboard reads — plus the ability to issue state-changing requests without the allowlist standing in the way.

One caveat worth stating: if this is the standard Express `cors` package, `origin: "*"` emits a literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, and browsers refuse to attach or expose cookies for such a response, so credentialed reads would fail (and the dashboard feature would not actually work as intended). The exposure is then limited to any data the endpoints return without cookie auth — which still includes anything protected only by network position or by IP. If the middleware is instead a wrapper that reflects the request origin when `credentials` is set, the credentialed cross-origin read is fully available and this is a complete bypass of the allowlist.

Fix: give the dashboard origin an explicit entry, e.g. `origin: [...ALLOWED, DASHBOARD_ORIGIN]` (or a function that checks the request origin against that list) and keep `credentials: true`. Never pair a wildcard with credentials.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true cannot work in browsers
findings.body:
The stated intent is to let the dashboard origin call the API *with cookies*, but this config sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. The Fetch spec forbids the wildcard when credentials mode is `include`: the browser fails the CORS check and the response is discarded, so every credentialed dashboard request breaks. The `cors` middleware passes `"*"` through literally — it does not reflect the request Origin — so no header rewriting saves this.

Fix by reflecting/allow-listing the actual dashboard origin instead, e.g. `origin: ["https://dashboard.example.com"]` (or a predicate function), keeping `credentials: true`. That is also the only form that is safe: if the wildcard *were* honoured, any site could read authenticated responses.

findings.title: dashboardCors contradicts itself without explanation
findings.body: The `dashboardCors` export combines `origin: "*"` (wildcard) with `credentials: true`. This is a known CORS misconfiguration: browsers will reject credential-bearing requests when the origin is a wildcard. A caller reading this code will see what appears to be a working configuration and may assume it functions as written. A comment explaining the intended behavior, why this pattern exists despite the contradiction, or what the actual runtime behavior will be, is essential for anyone maintaining or using this export.

findings.title: No test covers dashboardCors behaviour
findings.body: The new dashboardCors export combines origin: "*" with credentials: true, which is an invalid/unsafe CORS configuration (browsers reject wildcard origin with credentialed requests). There is no test in this diff exercising dashboardCors, so a misconfiguration like this — or any future regression in it — would not be caught by any test suite.
