findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded, replacing env var lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is committed in source with an `acme_live_` prefix, and the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup was removed (the `import os` line is deleted). Anyone with read access to the repository — a contributor, a CI job that echoes the tree, a mirror, a leaked clone, or the public if the repo is ever opened — obtains a production payments credential and can issue charges, refunds, or read customer payment data against the live account.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at AcmePay immediately, since it is now in git history and rotating is required even after the commit is reverted; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or pull from your secret manager) and re-add `import os`; (3) purge the value from history or confirm with AcmePay that the old key is revoked.

findings.title: Live key is now fixed at import, removing per-environment config
findings.body:
Previously `acmepay.api_key` was read from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each deployment (and CI/test runs) supplied its own key, and a missing key failed loudly with a `KeyError` at call time. After this change `client()` unconditionally assigns the module-level constant, which is an `acme_live_...` key. Any environment that previously exported a test or staging key now silently issues real charges against the production account, and there is no longer any way to override the key without editing source.

Restore the environment lookup (optionally with an explicit default or a clear error when unset) so non-production environments cannot pick up the live credential.

findings.title: client() behavior change is untested
findings.body: client() now sets acmepay.api_key from a hardcoded constant instead of os.environ. No test calls client() and asserts acmepay.api_key (or the client's key) equals the expected value. The new tests/fixtures/acmepay.py only defines a fixture (fake_client/TEST_KEY) but contains no test function or assertion, so nothing in this PR would fail if client() were wired incorrectly (e.g. wrong constant name, key never assigned, or reverted to reading a stale env var).

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unverified, attacker-controlled tenant id
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, which skips signature checking entirely (and, in PyJWT, also disables the audience/expiry checks that depend on a verified token). Any client can craft an unsigned JWT with an arbitrary `tenant_id` and this function will return it. If the value is used to scope queries or authorise access, that is cross-tenant data access.

The module already has the correct primitive one line above: `claims_for` verifies with `public_key()` and `algorithms=["RS256"]`. Implement `tenant_of` on top of it, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. If the motivation was avoiding the key-store round-trip, cache the public key rather than dropping verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: New unverified-claims function has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes the JWT without verifying its signature and trusts the tenant_id claim. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a regression (e.g. accidentally trusting a forged token, or a future change accidentally enabling signature verification and breaking the intended behavior) would go undetected. Add a test that constructs a token with a known tenant_id (signed with an arbitrary/wrong key) and asserts tenant_of returns the expected value, plus a test confirming it does not raise on an invalid signature.

findings.title: Unguarded claim lookup raises KeyError for tokens without tenant_id
findings.body: `unverified["tenant_id"]` assumes the claim is present. A well-formed token issued without a `tenant_id` (service tokens, older issuers) will raise a bare `KeyError` out of an auth helper, which callers are unlikely to catch and which typically surfaces as a 500 rather than a 401/403. Use `.get("tenant_id")` and let the caller decide, or raise a domain-specific auth error.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates without require_owner ownership check
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` fetches the `PaymentMethod` by id straight from the caller-supplied `pm_id` and writes `billing_name` without ever calling `require_owner`. Any authenticated user can pass another user's `pm_id` and overwrite the billing name on that card. The tell is line 11: `user = current_user(request)` is computed and then never used — the authorisation call that was supposed to consume it is missing. Add `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` on line 12, matching the read path on line 6.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ update_payment_method mutates any pm_id without ownership check

findings.title: Public API lacks required authorization documentation
findings.body: The function `update_payment_method` is a public endpoint that mutates a payment method object. The repository convention (visible in `auth.py`) requires that "every object mutation must call" `require_owner()`. This function does not. A caller reading the code signature cannot determine whether authorization is enforced, and the absence of `require_owner()` contradicts the documented contract of how object mutations must be guarded in this codebase.

findings.title: No test exists for update_payment_method, including its ownership check
findings.body: update_payment_method is new and has zero test coverage in this diff. In particular, unlike the read path above it (line 6, which calls require_owner), this function never calls require_owner before mutating pm. If a test existed exercising an update by a non-owner, it would currently pass even though the method allows any signed-in user to update any other user's saved payment method — because nothing asserts on ownership enforcement. Add a test that a non-owner request to update_payment_method is rejected, mirroring the pattern that should exist for get_payment_method.

findings.title: Password reset endpoint left with no rate limit
findings.body:
`request_reset` is an unauthenticated entry point: the caller supplies `email` and the function calls `send_reset_email(email)` with no throttle after the decorator removal. Adversary: any anonymous remote client. What they control: the `email` value and the request rate. What they get: (a) mail-bombing/harassment of an arbitrary victim address, (b) account-enumeration or reset-token grinding at unbounded volume if response timing/content differs per address, (c) burning the sending domain's reputation and quota.

The PR rationale — "the email provider already throttles" — protects the provider's own infrastructure, not this application: provider throttling is typically global or per-sender, so it does not stop thousands of resets aimed at one victim, and when it does trip it degrades all outbound mail including legitimate resets (a denial of service on the reset flow itself). Restore a per-identifier limit (per source IP *and* per target email) at this handler, or point to an equivalent limiter applied upstream.

findings.title: No test guards against removal of rate limiting on password reset
findings.body: The diff removes the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator from `request_reset`, eliminating throttling on this endpoint. No test file is included in this change, and no repository context was retrieved showing an existing test that asserts rate-limiting behavior on this endpoint. If this removal is a mistake (e.g., the email provider's throttling does not adequately cover abuse scenarios), nothing would fail to signal it — the function still returns `{"sent": True}` regardless of call frequency.

findings.title: Preview reader skips _confined(), allowing reads outside EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
The existing reader resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` (line 14) before opening it; `read_export_preview` instead does a raw `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)`. `os.path.join` returns `name` unchanged when it is absolute (e.g. `/etc/passwd`), and performs no `..` normalisation, so `../../etc/passwd` resolves outside the export directory. Since the description says the preview path "reuses the same layout as download", the omission looks accidental. Replace line 20 with `path = _confined(name)` so both entry points share the same containment check.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Preview path skips _confined(), allowing path traversal / arbitrary read

findings.title: No test covers path confinement for read_export_preview
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the sibling function above which calls _confined(name). No test in this diff exercises this function with a traversal-style name (e.g. '../../etc/passwd') to confirm it is safe or unsafe. If this is a behavioral regression versus the download path, nothing here would fail to signal it.

findings.title: Ownership check removed: bulk_export leaks other tenants' reports
findings.body:
`bulk_export` now fetches every `Report` named in the caller-supplied `report_ids` and serialises it, with no tenant check. `api/auth.py` documents `require_owner` as mandatory: "Every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through this." Deleting the loop turns this endpoint into a direct object reference: any authenticated user of any tenant can enumerate or guess report IDs and receive the full `to_dict()` payload of another tenant's reports.

Authentication (`current_user`) is not authorisation. Restore the check, e.g. keep the `for report in reports: require_owner(user, report)` loop, or — if the loop was the performance problem — push the tenant filter into the fetch (`Report.get_many(report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) so the database enforces it in one query rather than dropping enforcement entirely.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer checks report ownership, leaking cross-tenant data

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public API authorization contract undocumented after change

findings.title: No test guards bulk_export's tenant isolation behavior
findings.body: bulk_export previously called require_owner(user, report) for each report; that call is removed here. No test file is included in this diff, and nothing in the shown context indicates an existing test exercises bulk_export with reports belonging to a different tenant. If the removal of the ownership check is wrong (i.e., callers are not in fact always pre-authorized), no test in this change would catch it — the function would simply return other tenants' data silently.

findings.title: search_customers bypasses parameterisation contract of execute()
findings.body:
`billing/db.execute` documents that `params` "must carry every caller value", and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `%s` placeholders plus a tuple. `search_customers` instead interpolates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL string and calls `execute(sql)` with no params at all.

Two concrete consequences:
1. Any caller value containing a single quote (a perfectly ordinary support search such as `O'Brien`) terminates the string literal and the statement fails or, with attacker-chosen input, executes injected SQL. Since `term` and `status` come from a support-facing search box, this is directly reachable.
2. It breaks the module's established call convention, so the query is not covered by whatever escaping/parameter handling the driver provides.

Rewrite using placeholders and let the driver bind, e.g.:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    return execute(
        "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s",
        (f"%{term}%", status),
    )
```

Note the wildcards belong in the bound parameter, not in the SQL text.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function violates documented query contract

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`term` and `status` are interpolated straight into the SQL string and the query is then passed to `execute(sql)` with no params. A caller value containing a single quote closes the literal and the rest is parsed as SQL, e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and `term = "%'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` reaches the driver as a second statement if multi-statement execution is enabled.

Use the same parameterised form as `get_customer` directly above, keeping the wildcards in the bound value rather than the SQL text:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

If `status` is meant to be a fixed enum, additionally validate it against an allowlist before binding.

findings.title: No test exercises search_customers
findings.body: search_customers builds a raw SQL string via f-string interpolation instead of using the parameterised execute() helper (contrast with get_customer at line 5, which passes params). There is no test in this diff verifying the query behaves correctly for normal input, escaping, or special characters like `%`, `_`, or quotes in term/status. If this were rewritten to use parameters correctly or incorrectly, no test would fail either way.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check enforced by the sibling sender
findings.body:
The existing delivery path validates the destination host against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` and raises `ValueError` before issuing the request (lines 8-10). `verify_endpoint` takes a caller-supplied `url` and passes it straight to `requests.get` with no host extraction and no allowlist check, so the invariant the module establishes one line earlier does not hold for this entry point. Since this is described as a tenant-registered URL, a tenant can point it at internal addresses (link-local metadata endpoints, localhost admin ports, internal service names) and observe the returned status code, turning this into an internal-network probe.

Extract the host and run it through the same `ALLOWED_HOSTS` gate before the request, ideally by factoring the check in lines 8-9 into a shared helper that both functions call. Also consider `allow_redirects=False`, since a permitted host can 302 to an internal one and re-introduce the same problem after the check has passed.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check and enables SSRF

findings.title: New verify_endpoint has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that performs an outbound HTTP GET based on a caller-supplied URL, unlike the sibling function above it which validates the host against ALLOWED_HOSTS before making a request. There is no test in this diff exercising verify_endpoint, so a bug (e.g. missing host validation, wrong status handling, or exception propagation) would not be caught by any existing test suite.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises on network failure instead of reporting it
findings.body: The function's evident contract is "return the status code of the endpoint", but `requests.get` raises (`ConnectionError`, `Timeout`, `TooManyRedirects`, `InvalidURL`) for exactly the cases a verification call is meant to detect — an unreachable or malformed tenant URL. Callers that treat the return value as an int will see an exception escape instead. Wrap the call and return a sentinel (or `None`) for transport failures, or document that the caller must catch `requests.RequestException`.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket created with all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) is paired with an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets all four controls to `false`. These four settings are the account/bucket-level backstop that makes it *impossible* for an ACL or bucket policy to grant access to `AllUsers`/`AuthenticatedUsers`. Turning them off on a bucket holding customer invoices means:

- Anyone who can call `PutBucketPolicy`, `PutBucketAcl` or `PutObjectAcl` on this bucket — a compromised CI role, an over-broad developer policy, or any application role with `s3:Put*` — can make the entire invoice corpus world-readable, and nothing at the bucket level will stop them.
- Any object uploaded with `public-read` (a common SDK/CLI default in copy-pasted code) becomes anonymously readable immediately, since `ignore_public_acls = false`.

The attacker is an unauthenticated internet user once any such ACL or policy lands; the intermediate actor is anyone holding even minor S3 write permissions, or an operator making a one-line mistake. What they get is customer invoice data (names, addresses, amounts, likely tax IDs).

Recommend setting all four to `true` for `invoices`, and adding `aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration` plus versioning. If this bucket genuinely needs to exist, it should also be raised separately from a marketing-assets PR: the description mentions only a public assets bucket, so a reviewer skimming this diff is being asked to approve an unannounced public-capable invoices bucket.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket added with all public-access protections disabled

findings.title: verify_acmepay uses == instead of hmac.compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same HMAC-SHA256 digest as `verify_stripe` but compares it with `==`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and so leaks the position of the mismatch through response time. An attacker who can submit repeated webhook deliveries can recover a valid signature byte by byte and forge webhook payloads. The function directly above it (line 7) already does this correctly. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function ships with no test
findings.body: verify_acmepay is a new public function with a subtly different (and weaker) comparison than verify_stripe, yet the diff adds no test exercising it. Without a test, a regression or the current use of '==' instead of hmac.compare_digest would go unnoticed by CI.

findings.title: 500 handler returns exception text and traceback to the client
findings.body:
`handle(exc)` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the 500 response. Anyone who can reach the API and provoke an unhandled exception (malformed JSON, oversized or wrong-typed parameters, an ID that triggers a DB error) reads back absolute source paths, module and framework versions, function names and local call structure — and, because exception messages frequently embed the failing statement or connection target, often the SQL text or a DSN that can include credentials. That is a free reconnaissance primitive for an unauthenticated attacker and it makes every subsequent attack (version-specific exploits, blind-injection oracles, path guessing for LFI) materially easier.

The on-call need is already met by the `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8, which puts the same traceback where only operators can read it. Keep the client-facing body opaque and correlate with a request/error ID instead, e.g. generate a UUID, log it alongside the exception, and return `{"error": "internal error", "error_id": eid}`. If you want the detail inline for local work, gate it on an explicit non-production debug flag rather than returning it unconditionally.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ format_exc() may not describe `exc`, or yields 'NoneType: None'

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response shape changed: new key and non-constant `error` value

findings.title: No test verifies error response now includes exception/traceback
findings.body: The `handle` function's return value changed from a generic error message to one embedding `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()`. No test file is included in this diff to assert the new response shape. If this were reverted or broken (e.g., traceback omitted, exc not stringified correctly), nothing would fail.

findings.title: Reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives the stored credential with a single unsalted MD5 pass. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly hash with no salt and no work factor, so any hash produced here is recoverable to plaintext with rainbow tables or a few seconds of offline cracking — unlike the bcrypt output from `hash_password` on line 7.

Adversary: anyone who obtains the credential table (SQL injection, a leaked backup, a read-only replica, a malicious insider). What they control: nothing — the weakness is in the stored value itself. What they get: the users' plaintext passwords, which are typically reused on other services.

Use the same primitive as the existing path: `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())`. If this helper exists only to produce a short-lived reset artifact rather than a stored password, it is misnamed and should be built from `secrets.token_urlsafe` plus a keyed HMAC/SHA-256 over the token, not MD5 over a password. Also note that a reset writing an MD5 digest into a column the login path verifies with bcrypt will either break login or force a verification fallback that accepts the weak format for every subsequent authentication.

findings.title: Reset hash format is incompatible with bcrypt verification path
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), while the new `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char hex MD5 digest. If both values land in the same stored field and are verified by a shared routine, `bcrypt.checkpw(raw, stored)` on an MD5 digest raises `ValueError: Invalid salt` rather than returning False, so the reset flow will error out instead of authenticating (or failing cleanly). Either route reset credentials through `hash_password` so one verification routine works for both, or store a scheme tag alongside the digest and dispatch on it. Note also that the digest is unsalted, so identical reset secrets produce identical stored values.

findings.title: New hash_reset_password function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password introduces a new hashing behavior for password resets but no test in this diff exercises it. If the implementation were changed (e.g. to fix the weak hash, or if it silently returned an incorrect/empty digest), nothing in the test suite would fail. At minimum a test verifying the function returns a stable, non-trivial hash for known input would catch regressions.

findings.title: checksum() loads the entire file into memory
findings.body: `fh.read()` materialises the whole file before hashing, so memory use scales with file size and a large upload can exhaust the process. Hash in fixed-size blocks instead, e.g. iterate `iter(lambda: fh.read(1 << 20), b"")` and call `h.update(chunk)`.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs forked PR code with NPM_TOKEN in env
findings.body:
This change combines the three ingredients of a "pwn request":

1. `pull_request_target` (line 4) runs the workflow in the context of the *base* repository, so `secrets` are available and the injected `GITHUB_TOKEN` is a write-capable token for this repo — unlike `pull_request`, which gives forks no secrets and a read-only token.
2. `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` (line 12) checks out the attacker's commit, so the working tree is fully attacker-controlled, including `scripts/measure.sh`.
3. `./scripts/measure.sh` is then executed (line 13) with `NPM_TOKEN` in its environment (lines 14–15).

Adversary: any GitHub user, with no prior access, who opens a pull request from a fork. What they control: the entire contents of the checked-out tree at `head.sha`, including the script being run. What they get: the plaintext `NPM_TOKEN` (exfiltrable with a single `curl` line in the script) and, in the same step, a base-repo `GITHUB_TOKEN` they can use to push code or alter releases. Note this triggers on PR *open*, before any maintainer review, so "we'd notice the diff" is not a control.

Options, roughly in order of safety:
- Revert to `pull_request`. Forks still get CI signal; they just get no secrets. If the size check needs no credentials, drop the `NPM_TOKEN` env entirely and this is the right answer.
- If a credential really is required, split into two workflows: an unprivileged `pull_request` job that builds and uploads an artifact, and a `workflow_run` job that consumes the artifact and holds the secret, never executing fork code.
- If `pull_request_target` must stay, do not check out or execute fork-controlled code in the privileged job. At minimum add `permissions: contents: read` and gate the privileged path behind an explicit maintainer-applied label plus `environment:` approval — but note that even then, executing `scripts/measure.sh` from the fork checkout defeats the gate once approved for one commit if the PR can be updated.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target + checkout of PR head executes fork code with secrets

findings.title: pull_request_target workflow definition is taken from the base branch
findings.body: With `pull_request_target`, GitHub evaluates the workflow file as it exists on the base branch, not on the PR head. This change therefore has no effect on pull requests opened before it lands, and — more importantly for the stated goal — the job's steps can never be validated by the PR that edits them. If the intent was simply "external contributors get the same CI signal", `pull_request` already runs on forked PRs (it just does so without secrets and with a read-only token), so the trigger change is not what enables fork coverage; the secret on line 15 is the only thing `pull_request` would withhold. Confirm that `measure.sh` actually needs `NPM_TOKEN` before accepting the trigger change at all.

findings.title: Contexts that are hashable but not JSON-serialisable now raise TypeError
findings.body: The previous key `tuple(sorted(context.items()))` only required context values to be hashable and keys to be mutually comparable. `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)` additionally requires every value to be JSON-serialisable, so any existing caller passing a `datetime`, `Decimal`, `set`, tuple-keyed dict, or an arbitrary object into the context will now fail with `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` — a call that used to render fine. If the digest key is the goal, serialise with a fallback (`default=repr`) or hash a deterministic encoding of `repr`/`pickle` of the sorted items rather than strict JSON.

findings.title: No test covers non-JSON-serializable context values
findings.body: The old key was `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, which worked for any hashable context values (e.g. tuples, custom hashable objects, non-string dict keys). The new key uses `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`, which raises `TypeError` for non-JSON-serializable values and requires all dict keys to be strings (or coercible). This is a behavior change — contexts that previously worked will now raise — but none of the new tests exercise a context with such values, so a regression here would go undetected.

findings.title: No test asserts the constructed argv list, only shell=False
findings.body: The new implementation's safety depends on the exact argv list — specifically the `--` separator before `directory`, which prevents `directory` from being interpreted as a tar option (e.g. a directory value starting with `-`). test_runs_without_a_shell only checks `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`; it never inspects `spy.last_call.args` (the command list) to confirm the `--` separator, the correct ordering of `tar -czf /exports/<name>.tar.gz -- <directory>`, or that `directory` is passed as a single list element rather than being string-interpolated. If a future edit dropped the `--` separator or re-introduced string formatting for `directory` while keeping shell=False, none of the existing tests would fail.

findings.title: `directory` argument still unvalidated — possible arbitrary-path archiving
findings.body:
`name` is now tightly allowlisted, but `directory` flows straight into the `tar` argv with no constraint. The `--` on line 12 correctly stops it being read as an option flag, so flag injection is not possible; what remains is that the value is used verbatim as the *path to archive*. If any caller derives `directory` from a request parameter, an attacker supplies `/etc` or `../../home/app/.ssh` and then retrieves `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, turning this into arbitrary file read. Consider resolving the path and asserting it stays under an expected export root (`Path(directory).resolve().is_relative_to(EXPORT_ROOT)`), mirroring the validation already applied to `name`.

If `directory` is only ever supplied by internal, non-user-controlled code, this is not exploitable and can be closed — I could not establish the caller.

findings.title: `directory` is no longer word-split or glob-expanded by the shell
findings.body:
Previously the command string was handed to `/bin/sh`, so a `directory` value like `/srv/data/*`, `/srv/a /srv/b`, or anything containing whitespace was expanded/split by the shell and tar received multiple operands. With the list form plus `--`, the whole string is passed to tar as one literal path operand, so such callers now get `tar: /srv/data/*: Cannot stat: No such file or directory` and, with `check=True`, a `CalledProcessError` instead of an archive.

If any caller relies on globbing or multiple space-separated paths, change the signature to accept a sequence of directories (`*directories` or a list) and splat it into the argv, or document/assert that `directory` must be a single literal path.

findings.title: Tests depend on a `spy` fixture that is not part of this change
findings.body:
`test_runs_without_a_shell` requests a `spy` fixture, but no `conftest.py` or fixture definition is included in the diff. If it does not already exist in the repo, the test errors with `fixture 'spy' not found`. Worse, if `spy` exists but does not actually patch `subprocess.run`, this test really invokes `tar` and writes `/exports/nightly.tar.gz` on the machine running the suite, and will fail with `CalledProcessError` wherever `/srv/data` or `/exports` is absent.

Add the fixture (or a `monkeypatch.setattr(subprocess, "run", ...)`) alongside the test so the suite is self-contained, and assert the argv list itself — that the first positional argument is a `list` containing the exact `/exports/nightly.tar.gz` path — which is the property the change is really about; `shell is False` alone does not prove the command was not concatenated.

findings.title: New name allowlist rejects previously-valid archive names
findings.body:
`SAFE_NAME` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` and at most 64 characters. Names that worked before — anything containing a dot (`report.2024`), a space, a colon (common in timestamped names, e.g. `backup-2024-01-01T03:00`), or longer than 64 characters — now raise `ValueError` at call time rather than producing an archive. This turns a previously succeeding call into an exception for existing callers.

If timestamped or dotted names are in use, widen the character class (e.g. add `.` and `:`) and reconsider the 64-character cap, or confirm from the call sites that the stricter set is safe.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing
findings.body:
`test_renders_empty_invoice` calls `render(Invoice(lines=[]))` and discards the result without any assertion. The only failure mode it can detect is an uncaught exception; if `render` returns `None`, an empty string, a stray header, or garbage for the empty-lines case, the test still passes. Since this is the boundary case the other two tests deliberately skip, it is exactly the case that needs a concrete expectation — assert on the returned string (e.g. that it equals the expected empty-invoice rendering, or at minimum that it is a non-None string with a zero total).

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

findings.title: Mock-only assertion never checks rendered output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items patches format_line and only asserts fmt.call_count == 2. It never checks what render() actually returns or that the formatted lines appear in the output. If render() drops the formatted lines, joins them incorrectly, or renders them in the wrong order, this test still passes as long as format_line is called twice. Assert on the actual rendered string containing the expected line content instead.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test verifies only the mock, not the rendered output

findings.title: Failing test deleted with no accompanying rounding fix or replacement
findings.body:
The PR description says "fix the rounding and drop the failing test", but the only change in this diff is the removal of `test_rounds_half_to_even`. No production code is modified, so either the fix is missing from this changeset or the behaviour was changed elsewhere and this is the only trace. Either way, the exact-half rounding case (`Decimal("2.345")`) now has zero coverage: whichever direction `round_cents` rounds a tie, nothing asserts it. If the intent was to switch from half-to-even to half-up, add a replacement test asserting the new expected value (e.g. `== Decimal("2.35")`) rather than deleting the boundary case, and include the implementation change in this PR.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Deleted test for 2.345 rounding not replaced with corrected assertion

findings.title: Mock patches wrong target; retry test exercises real deliver
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` uses `from notify.transport import deliver`, so `deliver` is resolved from the `notify.sender` module namespace at call time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds only the attribute on the transport module and leaves `notify.sender.deliver` pointing at the original function. The test therefore calls the real `deliver` three times (possible real I/O, and a pass/fail that depends on the live transport rather than on the retry logic).

Use the same target as the existing test on line 2: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`. Consider also asserting the call count is 3 so the give-up-after-N behaviour is actually covered.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; test doesn't exercise retry logic

findings.title: Test patches wrong target, contradicting module documentation
findings.body: The new test on line 7 patches `notify.transport.deliver`, but the module docstring in `notify/sender.py` explicitly explains that this patch target will not work: '`deliver` is bound into this module's namespace at import time, so patching `notify.transport.deliver` does not affect it.' The test should patch `notify.sender.deliver` instead, as demonstrated by the first test on line 2. The current test will not actually exercise the retry-on-failure path as intended.

findings.title: csv_rows joins fields without applying csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with a bare `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)`, so a field whose value contains a comma or a double quote produces extra columns or unbalanced quoting, and the row no longer round-trips through any CSV parser. The `csv_escape` helper added ten lines below is exactly the fix but is never called. Wrap the stringified value: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ csv_rows joins fields without using the csv_escape helper

findings.title: csv_escape raises on non-str input and ignores embedded newlines
findings.body: Two boundary problems in the same function. (1) `"," in value` raises `TypeError: argument of type 'int' is not iterable` for any non-string cell (a numeric or `None` value from a row dict), so callers must remember to stringify first — coerce inside with `value = str(value)` or document the precondition. (2) A value containing `\n` or `\r` also needs quoting under RFC 4180; as written an embedded newline splits the record in two. Extend the condition to `if any(ch in value for ch in ',"\n\r')`.

findings.title: dump_streaming requires a sized sequence and emits nothing for empty input
findings.body: `len(rows)` and `rows[i : i + chunk_size]` mean this generator cannot accept the iterator/generator that a "streaming" entry point invites callers to pass — it raises `TypeError` instead. Separately, when `rows` is empty the loop body never runs and the generator yields zero chunks, so a consumer that concatenates the output gets an empty string rather than `"[]"`; the sibling `dump([])` returns `"[]"`, making the two entry points disagree on the empty case. Either document the sized-sequence precondition and the empty-input behaviour, or use `itertools.islice` and yield `"[]"` when there is nothing to emit.

findings.title: New CSV row/escape functions have no tests (and 2 more)
findings.body:
csv_rows and csv_escape are new public functions with no accompanying tests. The repo already tests csv_header at this level of granularity (test_csv.py), so the same standard should apply here — e.g. verify csv_rows respects column order/missing keys, and csv_escape correctly quotes commas/quotes.

The same gap appears at 2 other place(s) in this change:

- `reports/json_export.py:8` — New JSON export functions (dump_streaming, dump_pretty) untested
- `reports/pdf_export.py:5` — New PDF margin/width calculations untested

findings.title: Date comparison races the UTC midnight boundary (flaky test)
findings.body:
`issue_token()` captures `issued_at` at one instant and line 11 compares it against a *second* call to `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. If the first call lands just before 00:00:00 UTC and the second just after, `.date()` differs by one day and the assertion fails — an intermittent CI failure that is nearly impossible to reproduce. Freeze or inject the clock (e.g. a `now=`/clock parameter on `issue_token`, or a time-freezing fixture) and assert against that fixed instant, the same way `test_token_expires_after_an_hour` passes an explicit `now=` on line 6.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ New test depends on real-time clock, unlike sibling test

findings.title: Expired-coupon rejection path is untested
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) exercises a non-expired coupon. If the expiry comparison were inverted, removed, or the exception type/message wrong, no test would fail. Add a test asserting CouponExpired is raised for an expired coupon.

findings.title: apply_coupon now requires coupon.expires_at; missing/None value raises
findings.body: `apply_coupon` previously only read `coupon.amount`; it now unconditionally dereferences `coupon.expires_at`. Any existing caller or stored coupon without that attribute raises `AttributeError`, and a coupon with `expires_at=None` (the natural encoding of "never expires") raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'` — both surface as a 500 rather than a clean rejection. Guard the check, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now: raise ...`, and confirm every coupon source populates the field.
